In a running race, the “reaction time” is the time from the moment the starter’s pistol is fired until the runner leaves the starting blocks. The “final time” includes both the reaction time and the running time.

The table below shows the results of 8 athletes who ran the 100 meters at a regional youth competition (the results are made up for learning purposes).

Lane | Reaction time (s) | Final time (s)
1 | 0.152 | 10.35
2 | 0.141 | 10.22
3 | 0.188 | 10.47
4 | 0.205 | Did not finish
5 | 0.173 | 10.12
6 | 0.226 | 10.27
7 | 0.164 | 10.40
8 | 0.199 | 10.31
s0003: Comparing decimals from a table and ordering the smallest final times
s0004: The winner is the athlete with the smallest final time. Look only at the “Final time” column and leave out the runner who did not finish.
s0005: The athletes in which lanes won the gold, silver and bronze medals? (order: gold, silver, bronze)
s0007: The medal is decided by the final time, not the reaction time — and it must be as small as possible.
s0008: Lane 4 did not finish — not counted
s0009: The athlete in lane 4 did not finish the race, so we leave them out.
s0010: Let’s write the final times in increasing order: 10.12 (lane 5), 10.22 (lane 2), 10.27 (lane 6).
s0012: So gold goes to lane 5, silver to lane 2, and bronze to lane 6.
s0013: These are the fastest reaction times (0.141; 0.152; 0.164). An athlete can react quickly and still run slowly.
s0014: You subtracted the reaction time and compared the pure running times. But medals are awarded by final time.
s0015: These are the largest final times — that is, the last places. The smaller the time, the better the result.
s0016: Work out what is being measured in the race: the winner is decided by the final time.
s0017: Recalculating a time in a hypothetical situation and justifying the result by comparison
s0018: Subtract the actual reaction time from the final time to find the running time, then add the smallest possible reaction time to it.
s0019: So far, no human has been able to respond to the starting signal faster than 0.110 seconds. If the bronze medalist had reacted faster, could he have won the silver medal? Which answer is correct and correctly justified?
s0020: No: his final time is 10.27 s, which is greater than the silver medalist’s 10.22 s, and the reaction time does not change that.
s0021: Yes, he would even have won gold, because 10.154 s < 10.12 s.
s0022: Yes: in the best case it would be 10.27 − 0.226 + 0.110 = 10.154 s, which is less than 10.22 s.
s0023: No: 10.27 − 0.110 = 10.16 s, which is still more than the winner’s 10.12 s.
s0025: The bronze medalist is in lane 6: final time 10.27 s, reaction time 0.226 s.
s0026: His pure running time is 10.044 seconds.
s0028: We add the fastest possible reaction time, 0.110 s.
s0029: That is less than the silver medalist’s 10.22 s, but more than the gold medalist’s 10.12 s.
s0031: So he could have won silver, but not gold.
s0032: The final time includes the reaction time. If the reaction time gets shorter, the final time gets shorter too.
s0033: The comparison is wrong: 10.154 seconds is greater than 10.12 seconds, so it would not be gold.
s0034: Two mistakes: you removed the reaction time completely instead of replacing it with 0.110, and you compared with gold instead of silver.
s0035: First ask “what changes and what stays the same?”: the reaction time changes, but the running time stays the same.

At a country house near Charvak, a water tank has been installed for watering the garden. The lower part of the tank is a cylinder (height 1.2 m, diameter 1.0 m), and the upper part is a truncated cone that narrows toward the top (height 1.0 m, top opening diameter 0.2 m). The shape and dimensions are shown in the picture.

At first the tank is empty. Then a pump starts filling it with water at 2 liters per second.
s0039: Choosing the graph of water level against time based on the shape of the tank
s0040: For each part, think “how much does the level rise in 1 second?”: where the tank is wide, slowly; where it is narrow, quickly.
s0041: Which graph correctly shows how the height of the water level changes over time?
s0044: Graph A: one straight line from start to finish
s0045: Graph B: first a straight line, then a curve that gets steeper and steeper
s0046: Graph C: first a steeply rising curve, then a straight line
s0047: Graph D: first a straight line, then a horizontal line
s0049: The same amount of water flows into the tank every second.
s0051: In the lower cylinder the width does not change, so the level rises steadily — the graph is a straight line.
s0053: The upper part keeps narrowing, so 2 liters of water make a taller and taller layer — the graph gets steeper and steeper.
s0054: Answer: B) straight line, then a steeper curve
s0056: This is true only if the whole tank has the same width. The upper part narrows, so the level rises faster.
s0057: This fits a tank that is narrow at the bottom and then widens (for example, a cylinder on top of a cone with its tip at the bottom).
s0058: A horizontal line means the level has stopped rising, but water is still being pumped in.
s0059: Where the shape is wide, the level rises slowly; where it is narrow, it rises quickly — connect this to the slope of the graph.
s0060: A game at the Navruz fair
s0061:
At the Navruz fair, a game is played like this: the player first spins a spinner divided into 6 equal sections. If the spinner stops on an even number, the player gets to take one ball from a bag without looking. The spinner and the balls in the bag are shown in the picture: there are 16 balls in the bag, and 4 of them are black.

If a black ball comes out, the player wins a prize. Malika plays the game once.
s0064: Estimating the probability of a two-stage random event
s0065: Find the probability of each stage separately and multiply them, then describe the result in words.
s0066: How likely is it that Malika wins a prize?
s0072: Of the 6 numbers on the spinner, 5 are even; only 3 is odd.
s0074: So the probability of getting to take a ball from the bag is 5/6 — quite high.
s0076: Of the 16 balls in the bag, 4 are black.
s0077: Both conditions must happen, so the probabilities are multiplied: about 21%.
s0079: 21% is not impossible, but it is much less than 50%, so it is unlikely.
s0080: There are black balls and an even number can come up, so winning is possible.
s0081: You also need to look at the second stage: the probability of a black ball is only 1/4, and the overall probability is about 21%.
s0082: You looked only at the spinner (5/6). To win the prize, a black ball must also come out.
s0083: In a multi-stage game, each stage has a probability less than 1, so the overall probability gets smaller.
s0085: Zarina is swinging on a swing in the mahalla park. At some point she stops pumping with her legs, and now nobody is pushing the swing. The swing keeps going back and forth, but each time it rises a little lower than before. The lowest point of the swing is always at the same height.
s0086: Connecting real motion to a graph: decreasing amplitude of oscillation
s0087: Check two things: how the highest points change, and where the lowest points stay.
s0088: Which graph best shows how the height of Zarina’s feet above the ground changes over time?
s0095: The swing moves back and forth, so the graph is wave-shaped.
s0097: Since nobody pushes it, it rises lower each time — the peaks get lower.
s0099: The lowest point is always at the same height — the dips are all at one level.
s0100: Answer: B) peaks decrease, bottom level stays the same
s0101: Only graph B fits both conditions.
s0102: In A the peaks keep increasing — that is a child pumping and swinging higher and higher.
s0103: In C the swinging does not change, but the swing is slowing down and rising lower.
s0104: In D the lowest points keep rising. But the lowest point of the swing is always at the same height.
s0105: Before choosing a graph, write down the most important features of the motion in words.

The heights of all members of the neighborhood basketball club were measured. The boys’ mean height was 165 cm, and the girls’ was 155 cm. The tallest member is Jasur (182 cm), and the shortest is Malika (138 cm).

A week later, 2 more new members joined the club. Their heights were also measured and the means were recalculated. Interestingly, neither the boys’ nor the girls’ mean height changed.
s0108: Using properties of the arithmetic mean to decide which conclusion must be true
s0109: Look for a counterexample to each conclusion. If the conclusion fails in at least one possible case, it is not necessarily true.
s0110: Which of the following conclusions must follow from the given information?
s0111: One of the new members is a boy and the other is a girl.
s0112: The overall mean height of all club members did not change.
s0113: Malika is still the shortest member of the club.
s0114: If both new members are boys, their mean height is 165 cm.
s0115: If the mean doesn’t change: new value = mean
s0116: If you add a value equal to the mean to a group, the mean does not change.
s0117: A: they could also be 2 girls (155 and 155)
s0118: The condition still holds if both are girls, so A is not necessarily true.
s0119: B: adding 165 + 155 may change the overall mean
s0120: The overall mean depends on the numbers of boys and girls, so it can change.
s0121: C: a new member could be 135 cm
s0122: If one new girl is 135 cm and the other is 175 cm, the mean stays 155, and Malika is no longer the shortest.
s0124: If two boys join and the mean stays 165, their heights add up to 330, so their mean is 165.
s0126: So only conclusion D is true in every case.
s0127: Both could be girls (for example, 150 and 160 cm) or both could be boys — the condition would still hold.
s0128: For example, if two people of 165 cm and 155 cm join a group of 3 boys and 7 girls, the overall mean changes.
s0129: Even if one new girl is shorter than 138 cm and the other is tall, the girls’ mean can stay at 155.
s0130: Pay attention to the word “must”: one counterexample is enough to reject a conclusion.
s0132:
The apartment owners in one entrance of an apartment building agreed to repair the roof. They will share the cost in proportion to the floor area of each apartment.

For example, a family whose apartment makes up one fifth of the total floor area of all the apartments also pays one fifth of the total cost.
s0133: Evaluating properties of direct proportion in a real situation
s0134: “In proportion to the area” means everyone pays the same amount per 1 m². Check each statement against this rule.
s0135: Which of the following statements is correct?
s0136: The owner of the largest apartment pays more per 1 m² than the owner of the smallest apartment.
s0137: If we know the total cost and how much each family pays, we can calculate the total floor area of the apartments.
s0138: If the price of the repair goes up by 20%, each family’s payment also goes up by 20%.
s0139: If the price of the repair goes up by 20%, each family’s payment goes up by the same amount of money.
s0141: Proportional sharing: the price per 1 m² is the same for everyone.
s0142: A: same price per 1 m² → A is wrong
s0143: The owner of a large apartment pays more in total, but the same per 1 m².
s0144: B: only amounts of money → area unknown
s0145: Amounts of money do not tell us the area, so the total area cannot be found.
s0147: If the total amount goes up by 20%, each share also goes up by 20%.
s0149: D is wrong: the payments go up by the same percentage, not by the same amount.
s0150: With proportional sharing, the price per 1 m² is the same for everyone; only the total payment differs.
s0151: From the amounts of money we only know the shares, not the square meters.
s0152: The owner of a large apartment sees a bigger increase: payments do not all go up by the same amount, but by the same percentage.
s0153: With proportional sharing, a percentage change affects everyone by the same percentage.
s0154: Dividing a total amount in proportion to areas
s0155: First find the total area, then calculate the amount per 1 m².
s0156: There are three apartments in the entrance: apartment 1 is 72 m², apartment 2 is 64 m², and apartment 3 is 54 m². The roof repair costs 47 500 000 soums in total. How many soums should the owner of apartment 2 pay?
s0158: First, we add up the areas of all the apartments.
s0160: Each square meter costs 250 thousand soums.
s0161: Apartment 2 is 64 m², so we multiply 250 thousand soums by 64.
s0163: The owner of apartment 2 pays 16 million soums.
s0164: A common mistake is to divide the amount equally by 3 (15 833 333) or to divide 64 by 72 instead of by the total area. The payment equals the 64/190 share.
s0165: Check your result: the three payments must add up to the total cost.

A children’s clothing store has a chart on the wall for finding the clothing size that matches a child’s height.

Height (cm) from | to | Clothing size
99 | 104 | 26
105 | 110 | 28
111 | 116 | 30
117 | 122 | 32
123 | 128 | 34
129 | 134 | 36
135 | 140 | 38
141 | 146 | 40
147 | 152 | 42
153 | 158 | 44
s0168: Finding the needed value in a table of intervals
s0169: Find which interval (between “from” and “to”) the height falls into, and read the size in that row.
s0170: Dilnoza is 137 cm tall. According to the chart, what clothing size fits her?
s0173: We look for the row in the table that contains the number 137.
s0174: 137 is in the interval from 135 to 140.
s0176: The last column of this row says 38.
s0179: Students often take the neighboring row (36 or 40) or confuse the height with the size. 137 is exactly in the 135–140 interval.
s0180: In interval tables, always check both boundaries.

In the school chess club, Aziz, Bekzod, Dilshod and Sardor formed a practice group. Each student wants to play each of the others exactly once. They have been given two chessboards, so two games are played at the same time in each round.

Round 1: Board 1 Aziz – Bekzod, Board 2 Dilshod – Sardor.
s0183: Combinatorics: distributing all pairs into rounds without repetition
s0184: First count all the pairs (4 people give 6 pairs), cross out the ones from round 1, and arrange the rest so that everyone plays once in each round.
s0185: Which schedule for rounds 2 and 3 is correct?
s0186: Round 2: Aziz – Dilshod, Bekzod – Sardor; Round 3: Aziz – Bekzod, Dilshod – Sardor
s0187: Round 2: Aziz – Dilshod, Aziz – Sardor; Round 3: Bekzod – Dilshod, Bekzod – Sardor
s0188: Round 2: Aziz – Dilshod, Bekzod – Sardor; Round 3: Aziz – Sardor, Bekzod – Dilshod
s0189: Round 2: Aziz – Dilshod, Bekzod – Sardor; Round 3: Aziz – Sardor, Dilshod – Sardor
s0193: These have already been played. Remaining: Aziz–Dilshod, Aziz–Sardor, Bekzod–Dilshod, Bekzod–Sardor.
s0195: In one round, a student cannot play on two boards.
s0196: Round 2: Az–Dil, Bek–Sar; Round 3: Az–Sar, Bek–Dil
s0197: If we arrange them like this, every pair meets exactly once.
s0199: Round 3 repeats the games from round 1, and Aziz – Sardor and Bekzod – Dilshod are never played.
s0200: In one round, Aziz cannot play on two boards at the same time.
s0201: In round 3 Sardor plays twice, and the Bekzod – Dilshod game is left out.
s0202: When checking a schedule, ask two questions: is any game repeated? Does anyone play twice in one round?

On the shores of large reservoirs, signal lights are set up to guide boats at night. Each light flashes on and off in its own fixed, repeating pattern.

The picture shows the pattern of one of these lights: the upper line is the time when the light is on (light), and the lower line is the time when it is off (dark).

This pattern is regular: after a certain time it repeats exactly. The length of one complete cycle before the pattern starts repeating is called the “period”.
s0208: Finding the period from the graph of a periodic process
s0209: On the graph, find the point after which exactly the same sequence repeats from the start of the pattern.
s0210: Which of the following could be the period of this light’s pattern?
s0216: We read the segments of the graph one after another.
s0218: From the 6th second on, the same sequence repeats.
s0220: So one complete cycle is 6 seconds.
s0223: 2 seconds is only the first light segment. After 2 seconds the pattern continues differently.
s0224: From 0 to 3 seconds it is “2 s light, 1 s dark”, but from 3 to 6 it is “1 s light, 2 s dark” — these are not the same.
s0225: At 4 seconds it is dark, but at 0 seconds it was light — the pattern does not repeat after 4 s.
s0226: Once you have found the period, check the next cycle too — the pattern must match completely.
s0227: Using a value over one period to calculate a value over a longer time interval
s0228: Find how many seconds the light is on during one period, then calculate how many periods there are in 1 minute.
s0229: In total, how many seconds is the light on during 1 minute?
s0230: One period (6 s): light 2 s + 1 s = 3 s
s0231: In every 6 seconds, the light is on for 3 seconds in total.
s0233: There are 10 complete periods in one minute.
s0234: In 10 periods, it is light for 30 seconds.
s0237: 20 is the number of flashes in one minute (2 per period). But the question asks about the seconds the light is on.
s0238: You took both flashes as 2 seconds each. In fact, the second one is 1 second.
s0239: 10 is the number of periods in one minute, not the time the light is on.
s0240: Be clear about what the question asks: not the number of flashes, but the time the light is on.
s0241: Choosing a periodic pattern that meets given conditions (period and total time on)
s0242: For each pattern, check two things: is the period 5 seconds, and is the light on for 2 seconds in each period (60 : 5 · 2 = 24)?
s0243: Another light must be on for 24 seconds in total per minute, and its pattern must have a period of 5 seconds. Which of the patterns in the picture meets these conditions? (Upper line — light, lower line — dark.)
s0251: So in every 5 seconds, the light must be on for 2 seconds in total.
s0252: A: period 2; B: period 4; D: 3 s light
s0253: A and B do not have a period of 5, and D is light for 3 seconds per period.
s0255: In C the period is 5 s, and each period has 1 + 1 = 2 seconds of light.
s0256: Only pattern C meets the conditions.
s0257: In A the period is 2 s and there are 30 s of light per minute — both conditions fail.
s0258: In B the period is 4 s (2 s light + 2 s dark), with 30 s of light per minute.
s0259: D has a period of 5 s, but 3 s of light in each period — that makes 36 s per minute.
s0260: In problems like this, first go to “one period”: divide the total time by the number of periods.

Ecologists are worried that household waste keeps increasing. The table below shows the amount of household waste collected in one year in some regions in 2015 and 2023 (thousand tonnes), and the percentage change over that period. The numbers are hypothetical, for learning purposes.

Region | 2015 | 2023 | Change
Tashkent city | 1200 | 1380 | +15%
Samarkand reg. | 480 | 576 | +20%
Bukhara reg. | 260 | 299 | +15%
Navoi reg. | 150 | 189 | ?
Fergana Valley (total) | 1500 | 1470 | −2%
  including: Fergana reg. | 520 | 442 | −15%
  including: Andijan reg. | 460 | 497 | +8%
  including: Namangan reg. | 520 | 531 | +2%
s0263: Calculating the percentage change between two values
s0264: Find the change (new − old), divide it by the starting (old) value, and then multiply by 100.
s0265: The table does not show the percentage change for Navoi region. By what percentage did the amount of waste in Navoi region increase from 2015 to 2023?
s0267: First we find the change: it increased by 39 thousand tonnes.
s0268: We divide the change by the value for the starting year, 2015.
s0271: Waste in Navoi region increased by 26%.
s0272: A common mistake is to divide 39 by the 2023 value (189), which gives 21%. The divisor is the starting value, 150.
s0273: For a percentage change, the divisor is always the starting value.
s0274: Comparing percentage changes of a part and the whole to evaluate a claim
s0275: Remember that the change in the whole is the result of the changes in all its parts: some parts may increase while others decrease.
s0276: Malika looked at the table and said: “In Fergana region waste decreased by 15%, but in the whole valley by only 2%. That is impossible, because Fergana region is part of the valley.” Which statement is correct?
s0277: Malika is right: if a part decreases, the whole must decrease by at least the same percentage.
s0278: Malika is right: −15% + 8% + 2% = −5%, so the valley should show −5%.
s0279: Malika is right, because in 2023 the waste in the valley was more than 1500 thousand tonnes.
s0280: Malika is wrong: waste increased in Andijan and Namangan, so the decrease for the valley as a whole is smaller.
s0282: The valley as a whole is made up of three regions.
s0284: It decreased in one region and increased in two.
s0286: The increases make up for part of the decrease: 30 : 1500 = 2%.
s0288: So a part can decrease by more than the whole.
s0289: The whole is not made up of only one part: if other parts grow, the overall decrease is smaller.
s0290: You cannot simply add the percentages — each region has a different amount.
s0291: According to the table, the valley had 1470 thousand tonnes in 2023 — less than 1500.
s0292: To check a claim that something is “impossible”, calculate with the numbers in the table.
s0293: Distinguishing absolute and relative (percentage) growth and justifying two different correct conclusions
s0294: “The greatest increase” can be measured in two ways: in thousand tonnes (absolute) and in percent (relative). Find the largest in each.
s0295: Nodir: “Waste increased the most in Tashkent city.” Zarina: “No, it increased the most in Navoi region.” Which conclusion is correct?
s0296: Both are right: Tashkent had the largest increase in thousand tonnes (+180), and Navoi had the largest increase in percent (+26%).
s0297: Only Nodir is right: percentages are misleading, so only the tonnes should be compared.
s0298: Only Zarina is right: the regions are of different sizes, so only the percentages can be compared.
s0299: Both are wrong: the greatest increase was in Samarkand, because it is high on both measures.
s0301: The largest increase in thousand tonnes is in Tashkent: 1380 − 1200 = 180.
s0303: In the other regions the increase is much smaller.
s0305: The largest increase in percent is in Navoi, 26%.
s0307: Nodir meant absolute growth, and Zarina meant relative growth.
s0308: Measuring in tonnes is a valid method, but comparing by percentage is also valid — it shows relative growth.
s0309: Comparing by percentage is valid, but the absolute increase (in tonnes) is also a meaningful measure.
s0310: Samarkand is not first on either measure: Tashkent leads in tonnes, and Navoi leads in percent.
s0311: When there is a debate about data, first work out which measure each side is using.

In modern architecture, buildings often have unusual shapes. A “twisted tower” project is being considered in Tashkent (the project is hypothetical).

The ground (zero) floor of the building will contain the main entrance and shops. Above it there are 24 residential floors. The ground floor plan is a 40 m × 20 m rectangle; its long sides run from west to east. In the middle of the south wall there is a cylinder that contains the elevator (see the picture).

Every floor has the same plan as the ground floor, but each floor is rotated by the same angle counterclockwise about the center of the cylinder relative to the floor below it.
s0319: Estimating real measurements: estimating the height of a building from the number of floors and the height of one floor
s0320: Count the floors correctly (ground floor + residential floors) and use a realistic height for one floor (3–4 m).
s0321: Which range is the most realistic for the total height of the building?
s0323: We must not forget to include the ground floor — 25 floors in total.
s0325: A residential floor is about 3 meters high, and up to 4 meters including the slab between floors.
s0326: So the height is roughly 75 to 100 meters.
s0328: We choose the option that matches this range.
s0329: This assumes one floor is only 1–1.5 m high — a person could not stand up straight in such a room.
s0330: That is the height of a house with only 3–4 floors; the 25 floors were not taken into account.
s0331: This assumes one floor is 6–8 m high — far too tall for an ordinary residential building.
s0332: For an estimate, use your everyday experience: how many meters high is the ceiling in your room?
s0333: Finding an observer’s position from a plan and compass directions
s0334: Put yourself in the observer’s place: when you face the building, which compass direction is on your left?
s0335: An observer looks at the ground floor from ground level. They see only a narrow (20 m) wall of the building, and the elevator cylinder appears on the left side of that wall. From which direction is the observer looking at the building?
s0341: The long sides run from west to east, so the 20 m walls are on the west and east.
s0343: The elevator cylinder is in the middle of the south wall.
s0344: Looking from the east: facing west, south is on the left
s0345: When you face west, your left hand points south.
s0347: For the cylinder to appear on the left, the observer must be standing on the east side.
s0348: From the north, you would see the long (40 m) north wall, and the cylinder would be hidden behind the building.
s0349: Looking from the west, the observer faces east — south is on their right, so the cylinder appears on the right.
s0350: From the south, you would see the long south wall with the cylinder in the middle of it.
s0351: In spatial problems, check by rotating the drawing or by facing that direction yourself.
s0352: Working out which faces are visible when viewed from a corner
s0353: When viewed from a corner direction (for example, from the southwest), you see the walls that face those two directions.
s0354: Another observer looks at the ground floor from the southwest. Which two walls do they see, and is the elevator cylinder visible?
s0355: The south and west walls; the cylinder is visible
s0356: The north and east walls; the cylinder is not visible
s0357: The south and east walls; the cylinder is visible
s0358: The north and west walls; the cylinder is not visible
s0360: The observer is on the south side and the west side at the same time.
s0362: They see the walls that face those two directions.
s0363: Cylinder on the south wall → visible
s0364: The elevator cylinder is on the south wall, so it is visible too.
s0367: This is the view from the northeast — the opposite side from the observer.
s0368: The east wall is on the far side from the observer — it is visible from the southeast.
s0369: The north wall is on the back side of the building and cannot be seen from the southwest.
s0370: First name the directions where the observer is standing, then find the walls that face those directions.
s0371: Finding the rotation angle of an intermediate floor in a uniform twist
s0372: Find the rotation angle per floor (total rotation : number of floors), then multiply it by the number of the floor you need.
s0373: The top floor, floor 24, is rotated by 90° relative to the ground floor. By how many degrees is floor 16 rotated relative to the ground floor?
s0376: From the ground floor to floor 24 there is a total rotation of 90°.
s0378: Each floor is rotated by 3.75 degrees relative to the one below it.
s0379: Up to floor 16, there have been 16 rotations.
s0381: Floor 16 is rotated by 60° relative to the ground floor.
s0382: A common mistake is to assume floor 16 is in the middle and write 45°, or to divide 90° by 25 (the number of floors including the ground floor). There are 24 rotations.
s0383: Check your result: 16 is 2/3 of 24, so the angle is also 2/3 of 90° — 60°.

A city taxi service calculates the fare from the distance using a formula. For many years the following formula was used:

Old fare: Price = 8 000 + 1 500 · x  (soums, x — distance in km)

Recently the service changed its fares. The new formula is:

New fare: Price = 12 000 + 1 300 · x

A newspaper wrote: “The new fare is a little more expensive for short trips and a little cheaper for long trips.”
s0386: Setting two linear formulas equal to find the value beyond which one is smaller
s0387: Set the two formulas equal and find x; then check which fare is cheaper for distances greater than that point.
s0388: For trips longer than how many kilometers is the new fare cheaper than the old fare?
s0390: We find the distance at which the prices are equal.
s0391: We move the x terms to one side and the numbers to the other side.
s0393: At 20 km both fares are the same: 38 000 soums.
s0395: Let’s check: at 30 km the new fare is cheaper.
s0397: For trips longer than 20 km, the new fare is cheaper.
s0398: A common mistake is to divide 4 000 by 1 500 or by 1 300 (2.7 or 3.1 km). In the equation, the difference between the coefficients of x is 200.

s0449: The moving walkway at the airport
s0450: Large airports have moving walkways so that passengers can move quickly along long corridors. For one such walkway, 60 m long, the graph shows the motion of two people: one walks on the ordinary floor next to the walkway, and the other stands still on the moving walkway without walking.

s0461: From the graph: the person on the floor covers 60 meters in 48 seconds.

Mass | Price
up to 250 g | 12 000 soums
251 g – 500 g | 15 000 soums
501 g – 1000 g | 19 000 soums
1001 g – 2000 g | 26 000 soums
2001 g – 5000 g | 38 000 soums
5001 g – 10 000 g | 55 000 soums
s0473: Recognizing a piecewise-constant (step) relationship on a graph
s0474: Within one interval, the price does not change even if the mass changes. Think about what this looks like on a graph.
s0475: Which of the following graphs best represents the courier prices? (The horizontal axis is mass, the vertical axis is price.)
s0482: Price is constant within an interval

s0485: Each interval is a horizontal segment on the graph.
s0487: When you move to the next interval, the price suddenly goes up — this makes a step.

s0492: A straight line means the price depends evenly on the mass — but in the table the price changes in jumps.
